questions.label: 20-21 1(a)
questions.text: Define Inductance with the required expression.
questions.points: Inductance is flux linkage per ampere, $L = \psi/I = N\phi/I$ henry; it opposes a change of current, $e = L\,di/dt$; for a line, $L = 2\times10^{-7}\ln(D/r')$ H/m per conductor.
draws: Diagram: flux of one current-carrying conductor, inside and outside

questions.label: 21-22 TT1 7(a)
questions.text: A 500 kV line has a bundling arrangement of 2 conductors per phase as shown in the Figure 1. Compute the inductive reactance per phase of this line at 50 Hz. Each conductor carries 50% of the phase current.
questions.method: $r' = 0.7788r$; bundle $D_s = \sqrt{r'd}$; $D_{eq}$ from the bundle centres; $L = 2\times10^{-7}\ln(D_{eq}/D_s)$; $X_L = 2\pi fL$.
draws: Diagram: two-conductor bundle and its GMR

questions.label: 20-21 1(b)
questions.text: Each conductor of the bundled-conductor line shown in Fig.1 is ACSR, 1,272,000-cmil Pheasant. Find the inductive reactance in ohms per km (and per mile) per phase for d=45cm.
questions.method: Bundle GMR $D_s^b = \sqrt{D_sd}$ with the table $D_s$; $D_{eq} = \sqrt[3]{D_{ab}D_{bc}D_{ca}}$; $L = 2\times10^{-7}\ln(D_{eq}/D_s^b)$; $X_L = 2\pi fL$ at 50 Hz (handwritten on the scan).
draws: Diagram: two-conductor bundle and its GMR

questions.label: 21-22 5(b)
questions.text: A three phase 50 Hz transmission line has flat horizontal spacing with 3.5 m between adjacent conductors. The conductors are No. 2/0 hard/drawn seven strand copper (outside conductor diameter= 1.05 cm). The voltage of the line is 110 kV. Find the capacitance to neutral and the charging current per kilometre of line.
questions.method: $D_{eq} = \sqrt[3]{D\cdot D\cdot2D}$; $C_n = 2\pi\varepsilon_0/\ln(D_{eq}/r)$; $I_c = \omega C_nV_{ph}$.
draws: Diagram: three conductors in a horizontal row

questions.label: 21-22 5(d)
questions.text: Derive the expression of capacitance of a three phase line with unsymmetrical spacing.
questions.outline: Line charge: $V = (q/2\pi\varepsilon_0)\ln(D_2/D_1)$; $V_{ab}$ in the three transposition sections; average: the distances multiply, $D_{eq} = \sqrt[3]{D_{12}D_{23}D_{31}}$; same for $V_{ac}$; add with $q_a + q_b + q_c = 0$; $V_{ab} + V_{ac} = 3V_{an}$; $C_n = 2\pi\varepsilon_0/\ln(D_{eq}/r)$.
draws: Diagram: three charged conductors at unequal spacing
Diagram: one transposition cycle

questions.label: 21-22 TT1 7(b)
questions.text: Derive the expression for the capacitance of a three-phase line with unsymmetrical spacing.
questions.outline: Line charge: $V = (q/2\pi\varepsilon_0)\ln(D_2/D_1)$; $V_{ab}$ in the three transposition sections; average: the distances multiply, $D_{eq} = \sqrt[3]{D_{12}D_{23}D_{31}}$; same for $V_{ac}$; add with $q_a + q_b + q_c = 0$; $V_{ab} + V_{ac} = 3V_{an}$; $C_n = 2\pi\varepsilon_0/\ln(D_{eq}/r)$.
draws: Diagram: three charged conductors at unequal spacing
Diagram: one transposition cycle

questions.label: 20-21 1(c)
questions.text: Derive the expression of Capacitance of a three phase line with unsymmetrical spacing.
questions.outline: Line charge: $V = (q/2\pi\varepsilon_0)\ln(D_2/D_1)$; $V_{ab}$ in the three transposition sections; average: the distances multiply, $D_{eq} = \sqrt[3]{D_{12}D_{23}D_{31}}$; same for $V_{ac}$; add with $q_a + q_b + q_c = 0$; $V_{ab} + V_{ac} = 3V_{an}$; $C_n = 2\pi\varepsilon_0/\ln(D_{eq}/r)$.
draws: Diagram: three charged conductors at unequal spacing
Diagram: one transposition cycle

questions.label: 21-22 1(d)
questions.text: A single-phase 50 Hz power line is supported on a horizontal cross-arm. The spacing between the conductors is 3 m. A telephone line is supported symmetrically below the power line as shown in Fig. 1. Find the mutual inductance between the two circuits and the voltage induced per kilometer in the telephone line if the current in the power line is 100 A. Assume the telephone line current to be zero.
questions.method: $D_1$ and $D_2$ from the geometry of Fig. 1; $M = 4\times10^{-7}\ln(D_2/D_1)$ (both power wires add); $E = \omega MI$.
draws: Diagram: flux of the power wires linking the telephone loop

questions.label: 21-22 TT3 9(b)
questions.text: A single phase 50Hz power line is supported on a horizontal cross-arm. The spacing between conductors is 2.5m. A telephone line is also supported on a horizontal cross-arm in the same horizontal plane as the power line. The conductors of the telephone line are of solid copper spaced 0.6m between centers. The distance between the nearest conductors of the two lines is 20m. Find the mutual inductance between the circuits and the voltage per km induced in the telephone line for 150A current flowing over the power line.
questions.method: Distances from each power wire to each telephone wire; flux of $P_1$ and $P_2$ linking the telephone loop; $M = 2\times10^{-7}\ln[(D_{P_1T_2}D_{P_2T_1})/(D_{P_1T_1}D_{P_2T_2})]$; $E = \omega MI$.
draws: Diagram: power and telephone lines in one plane

questions.label: 20-21 1(d)
questions.text: A single phase 50Hz power line is supported on a horizontal cross-arm. The spacing between conductors is 2.5m. A telephone line is also supported on a horizontal cross-arm in the same horizontal plane as the power line. The conductors of the telephone line are of solid copper spaced 0.6m between centers. The distance between the nearest conductors of the two lines is 20m. Find the mutual inductance between the circuits and the voltage per km induced in the telephone line for 150A current flowing over the power line.
questions.method: Distances from each power wire to each telephone wire; flux of $P_1$ and $P_2$ linking the telephone loop; $M = 2\times10^{-7}\ln[(D_{P_1T_2}D_{P_2T_1})/(D_{P_1T_1}D_{P_2T_2})]$; $E = \omega MI$.
draws: Diagram: power and telephone lines in one plane

questions.label: 20-21 2(a)
questions.text: Define Corona Effect.
questions.points: Corona: violet glow, hissing, ozone and power loss round a conductor when the surface field exceeds the strength of air (30 kV/cm peak) and the air ionises. Depends on voltage, conductor size and surface, spacing and weather.
draws: Diagram: field lines and the ionised shell round a conductor
compare: Corona vs skin effect: air ionises round a high-voltage conductor vs ac current crowds to the conductor surface

questions.label: 21-22 1(c)
questions.text: Define transpose transmission line. Derive the expression for the inductance of three phase transmission lines with unsymmetrical spacing.
questions.outline: Flux of a line current $2\times10^{-7}I\ln(1/D)$; $\psi_a$ in the three sections; average: the distances multiply; $I_b + I_c = -I_a$; $\psi_a = 2\times10^{-7}I_a\ln(D_{eq}/r')$; $L = \psi_a/I_a$.
draws: Diagram: flux of one conductor
Diagram: one transposition cycle

questions.label: 20-21 2(b)
questions.text: Define Transposed Transmission line. Explain the reason behind Transpose.
questions.points: A transposed line exchanges conductor positions at intervals so each occupies each position for one third of the length. Reason: with unsymmetrical spacing the phases have unequal $L$ and $C$; transposition equalises them, keeps the voltage drops balanced and reduces telephone interference.
draws: Diagram: one transposition cycle

questions.label: 21-22 4(c)
questions.text: Derive the expression of inductance of composite conductor lines.
questions.outline: Flux of a line current $2\times10^{-7}I\ln(1/D)$, with $r'$ for itself; flux of strand $a$; combine the logs; $L_a = \psi_a/(I/n)$; every strand; $n$ strands in parallel, $L_X = \sum L/n^2$; mutual GMD over self GMD; loop $L = L_X + L_Y$.
draws: Diagram: composite conductors X ($n$ strands) and Y ($m$ strands)

questions.label: 20-21 2(c)
questions.text: Derive the expression of Inductance of composite conductor lines.
questions.outline: Flux of a line current $2\times10^{-7}I\ln(1/D)$, with $r'$ for itself; flux of strand $a$; combine the logs; $L_a = \psi_a/(I/n)$; every strand; $n$ strands in parallel, $L_X = \sum L/n^2$; mutual GMD over self GMD; loop $L = L_X + L_Y$.
draws: Diagram: composite conductors X ($n$ strands) and Y ($m$ strands)

questions.label: 21-22 2(c)
questions.text: A single core cable for use on 11 kV, 50 Hz system has conductor area of 0.645 cm$^2$ and internal diameter of sheath is 2.18 cm. The permittivity of the dielectric used in the cable is 3.5. Find: (i) the maximum electrostatic stress in the cable, (ii) minimum electrostatic stress in the cable, (iii) capacitance of the cable per km length, and (iv) charging current.
questions.method: $g_{max} = 2V/(d\ln(D/d))$ at the core, $g_{min} = 2V/(D\ln(D/d))$ at the sheath; $C = 2\pi\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r/\ln(D/d)$; $I_c = \omega CV$.
draws: Graph: stress across the insulation, largest at the core

questions.label: 21-22 TT2 8(b)
questions.text: A single core cable for use on 11 kV, 50 Hz system has a conductor area of 0.645 cm$^2$ and internal diameter of sheath is 2.18 cm. The permittivity of the dielectric used in the cable is 3.5. Find (i) the maximum electrostatic stress in the cable (ii) the minimum electrostatic stress in the cable (iii) the capacitance of the cable per km length (iv) the charging current.
questions.method: $g_{max} = 2V/(d\ln(D/d))$ at the core, $g_{min} = 2V/(D\ln(D/d))$ at the sheath; $C = 2\pi\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r/\ln(D/d)$; $I_c = \omega CV$.
draws: Graph: stress across the insulation, largest at the core

questions.label: 20-21 2(d)
questions.text: A 33 kV single core cable has a conductor diameter of 1 cm and a sheath of inside diameter 4 cm. Find the maximum and minimum stress in the insulation.
questions.method: $g_{max} = 2V/(d\ln(D/d))$, $g_{min} = 2V/(D\ln(D/d))$ with $V$ = 33 kV core to sheath.
draws: Graph: stress profile of this cable

questions.label: 20-21 3(c)
questions.text: Derive the expression of dielectric stress in a single core cable.
questions.outline: Gauss: $D_x = Q/2\pi x$; $g_x = Q/(2\pi\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_rx)$; integrate from $d/2$ to $D/2$: $V = (Q/2\pi\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r)\ln(D/d)$; remove $Q$: $g_x = V/(x\ln(D/d))$; $g_{max}$ at the core, $g_{min}$ at the sheath.
draws: Diagram: cable section with the Gauss cylinder

questions.label: 20-21 4(c)
questions.text: The maximum and minimum stresses in the dielectric of a single core cable are 40 kV/cm (r.m.s.) and 10 kV/cm (r.m.s.) respectively. If the conductor diameter is 2 cm, find : (i) thickness of insulation (ii) operating voltage
questions.method: $g_{max}/g_{min} = D/d$ gives $D$; thickness $(D - d)/2$; $V = g_{max}(d/2)\ln(D/d)$.
draws: Graph: stress across this cable

questions.label: 20-21 3(a)
questions.text: Define Skin Effect.
questions.points: Skin effect: alternating current crowds towards the surface because the inner filaments link more flux and have more reactance; the effective area falls, so the ac resistance exceeds the dc resistance; it grows with frequency, size and conductivity; stranded and hollow conductors reduce it.
draws: Diagram: current density across a conductor, dc and ac

questions.label: 20-21 3(b)
questions.text: Describe different FACTS devices and applications.
questions.points: FACTS controllers change $V$, $X$ or $\delta$ in $P = V_1V_2\sin\delta/X$. Shunt (SVC, STATCOM): voltage control and reactive support. Series (TCSC, SSSC): lower $X$, more power, flow control, damping. Combined (UPFC, IPFC): $V$, $X$ and $\delta$ together.
draws: Diagram: shunt, series and combined FACTS connections
compare: SVC vs STATCOM: thyristor-switched reactors and capacitors vs voltage-source converter, works at low voltage

questions.label: 20-21 3(d)
questions.text: The capacitances of a 3-phase belted cable are 12·6 μF between the three cores bunched together and the lead sheath and 7·4 μF between one core and the other two connected to sheath. Find the charging current drawn by the cable when connected to 66 kV, 50 Hz supply.
questions.method: Three cores bunched to sheath: $3C_s$ measured; one core to the other two and sheath: $C_s + 2C_c$; per-phase $C_N = C_s + 3C_c$; $I_c = \omega C_NV_{ph}$.
draws: Diagram: belted cable construction
Diagram: core-to-core and core-to-sheath capacitances

questions.label: 21-22 1(a)
questions.text: Define critical disruptive voltage. Write down it's significance.
questions.points: $V_c$: the least phase-to-neutral voltage at which the surface field reaches the breakdown strength of air (30 kV/cm peak) and corona starts, $V_c = m_0g_0\delta r\ln(d/r)$ kV; below it no corona; above it corona loss, interference and ozone; lines are designed below it.
draws: Diagram: field lines and the corona shell round a conductor

questions.label: 20-21 4(a)
questions.text: Define critical disruptive voltage. Write down its significance.
questions.points: $V_c$: the least phase-to-neutral voltage at which the surface field reaches the strength of air (30 kV/cm peak) and corona starts: $V_c = m_0g_0\delta r\ln(d/r)$ kV. Significance: above it corona loss, interference and ozone appear; lines are designed to work below it.
compare: Critical disruptive vs visual critical voltage: corona starts (no glow yet) vs the glow becomes visible, higher

questions.label: 21-22 3(c)
questions.text: In a 33 kV overhead line, there are three units in the string of insulators. If the capacitance between each insulator pin and earth is 11% of self capacitance of each insulator, find (i) the distribution of voltage over 3 insulators and (ii) String efficiency.
draws: Circuit: equivalent circuit of a three-disc string

questions.label: 21-22 3(d)
questions.text: Derive the mathematical expression of String efficiency with proper diagram. What will happen if: (i) $K = 0.2$ ($K = \frac{shunt~capacitance}{self~capacitance}$) (ii) $K = 0.8$ (iii) the number of disc increases in the string.
questions.outline: Each capacitance carries $\omega CV$; KCL at A: $V_2 = (1 + K)V_1$; KCL at B: $V_3 = (1 + 3K + K^2)V_1$; add for $V$; $\eta = V/(3V_3)$; evaluate at $K = 0.2$, 0.8 and for more discs.
draws: Graph: voltage share per disc for several $K$
Graph: efficiency against the number of discs

questions.label: 21-22 5(c)
questions.text: A 3-phase transmission line is being supported by three-disc insulators. The potentials across top unit (near to the tower) and middle unit are 8 kV and 11 kV, respectively. (i) Draw the equivalent circuit (ii) Calculate the ratio of capacitance between pin and earth to the self-capacitance of each unit (iii) Calculate the line voltage and (iv) Calculate string efficiency.
questions.method: $V_2 = (1 + K)V_1$ gives $K$; $V_3 = V_2 + K(V_1 + V_2)$; phase voltage = $V_1 + V_2 + V_3$; line voltage $\sqrt3$ times; $\eta = V/(3V_3)$.
draws: Circuit: equivalent circuit of the three-disc string with the measured voltages

questions.label: 21-22 TT2 8(a)
questions.text: A string of 5 insulators is connected across a 100 kV line. If the capacitance of each disc to earth is 0.1 of the capacitance of the insulator, calculate (i) the distribution of voltage on the insulator discs and (ii) the string efficiency.
questions.method: $V = 100/\sqrt3$ kV; $V_{k+1} = V_k + K(V_1 + \dots + V_k)$ for five discs; $V_1$ from the sum; $\eta = V/(5V_5)$.
draws: Graph: voltage on each disc of the five-disc string

questions.label: 20-21 4(b)
questions.text: What is String Efficiency? Discuss the methods of improving String Efficiency.
questions.points: $\eta = V/(nV_n)$; the shunt capacitance $KC$ makes the line unit take the most voltage, so $\eta < 100$ %. Improve it with longer cross-arms (smaller $K$), capacitance grading of the discs, and a guard (static shielding) ring at line potential.
draws: Circuit: equivalent circuit of a three-disc string
Diagram: three ways of improving string efficiency
Graph: efficiency against the number of discs

questions.label: 21-22 3(a)
questions.text: How electrical breakdown happen in a pin-type insulator?
questions.points: By flash-over (an arc through the air from the conductor to the pin; the insulator survives) or puncture (a discharge through the porcelain; destroyed). Safety factor = puncture strength / flash-over voltage, about 10, so flash-over comes first.
draws: Diagram: flash-over and puncture paths of a pin insulator
compare: Flash-over vs puncture: arc through the air outside, insulator survives vs discharge through the porcelain, insulator destroyed

questions.label: 20-21 5(a)
questions.text: What are the causes of insulation failure?
questions.points: Cracking from unequal expansion of porcelain, steel and cement; impure material; porosity; poor glazing; flash-over (arc heat cracks it); mechanical stress (tension, wind, ice); short circuits.
draws: Diagram: flash-over and puncture paths of a pin insulator
compare: Flash-over vs puncture: arc through the air outside, insulator survives vs discharge through the porcelain, insulator destroyed

questions.label: 21-22 1(b)
questions.text: In a test for a fault to earth on a 500 m length of cable having a resistance of 1 Ω per 1000 m, the faulty cable is looped with a sound cable of the same length but having a resistance of 2.25 Ω per 1000 m. The resistance of the other two arms of the testing network at balance are in the ratio of 2.75 : 1. Calculate the distance of the fault from the testing end of the cable.
questions.method: Loop resistance $R_{loop}$ = faulty + sound cable; at balance $R_X/(R_{loop} - R_X) = Q/P$, so $R_X = R_{loop}/(1 + P/Q)$; distance = $R_X$ / resistance per metre.
questions.answer: fault at 433.3 m from the testing end
draws: Circuit: Murray loop test

questions.label: 21-22 TT3 9(a)
questions.text: In a test for a fault to earth on a 500 m length of cable having a resistance of 1 Ω per 1000 m, the faulty cable is looped with a sound cable of the same length but having a resistance of 2.25 Ω per 1000 m. The resistance of the other two arms of the testing network at balance are in the ratio 2.75 : 1. Calculate the distance of the fault from the testing end of the cable.
questions.method: Loop resistance $R_{loop}$ = faulty + sound cable; at balance $R_X/(R_{loop} - R_X) = Q/P$, so $R_X = R_{loop}/(1 + P/Q)$; distance = $R_X$ / resistance per metre.
questions.answer: fault at 433.3 m from the testing end
draws: Circuit: Murray loop test

questions.label: 20-21 5(b)
questions.text: Varley loop test is performed to locate an earth fault on a 20 km long cable. The resistance per km of the single conductor is 20 ohm. The loop is completed with a similar healthy conductor. At balance, the variable resistance connected to the faulty conductor is 200 ohm. The fixed resistors have equal values. Calculate the distance of the fault from the test end.
questions.method: Varley loop: $R_{loop}$ = twice the cable resistance; with $P = Q$, $R_X = (R_{loop} - S)/2$; distance = $R_X$ / resistance per km.
draws: Circuit: Varley loop test
compare: Murray vs Varley loop test: ratio arms only, balance by $P/Q$ vs extra variable resistor $S$ in the faulty leg

questions.label: 21-22 4(a)
questions.text: What is Stringing charts?
questions.points: A stringing chart: curves of sag and tension against temperature for a given conductor and span; the lineman reads the right sag (or tension) for the temperature at erection, so the line is safe at both temperature extremes.
draws: Graph: sag and tension against temperature

questions.label: 20-21 5(c)
questions.text: A 132 KV transmission line has the following data: Weight of the conductor= 680 kg/km, Length of span= 260 m, Ultimate strength= 3100 kg, Safety Factor= 2. Calculate the height above ground at which the conductor should be supported. Ground clearance required is 10 meters.
questions.method: Working tension $T$ = ultimate strength / safety factor; sag $S = wl^2/(8T)$; support height = clearance + sag.
draws: Diagram: conductor between supports with sag and clearance

questions.label: 21-22 6(c)
questions.text: Explain what happens for sudden increase in mechanical input to generator using $Pe - \delta$ diagram.
questions.points: A sudden rise of $P_m$ makes $P_m > P_e$: the rotor accelerates, $\delta$ passes the new equilibrium $\delta_1$ (area $A_1$), overshoots to $\delta_2$ where the decelerating area $A_2 = A_1$, then swings back and, with damping, settles at $\delta_1$; unstable if $A_1$ exceeds the area available up to $180° - \delta_1$.
draws: Graph: $P_e$–$\delta$ curve with the accelerating and decelerating areas
Graph: rotor angle swing after the step

questions.label: 20-21 6(a)
questions.text: Define Power Angle. Briefly explain Equal Area Criterion.
questions.points: Power angle $\delta$: the angle between the internal emf and the infinite-bus voltage; $P_e = (EV/X)\sin\delta$. Equal area criterion: after a disturbance the machine stays in step if the decelerating area ($P_e > P_m$) can equal the accelerating area ($P_m > P_e$).
draws: Diagram: phasor diagram with the power angle
Graph: equal area criterion for a cleared fault

questions.label: 20-21 6(b)
questions.text: Explain what happens for sudden increase in mechanical input to generator using Pe-δ diagram.
questions.points: A sudden rise of $P_m$ makes $P_m > P_e$: the rotor accelerates, $\delta$ passes the new equilibrium $\delta_1$ (area $A_1$), overshoots to $\delta_2$ where the decelerating area $A_2 = A_1$, then swings back and, with damping, settles at $\delta_1$; unstable if $A_1$ exceeds the area available up to $180° - \delta_1$.
draws: Graph: $P_e$–$\delta$ curve with the accelerating and decelerating areas
Graph: rotor angle swing after the step

questions.label: 21-22 6(d)
questions.text: The generator of Fig. 2 is delivering 1.0 pu power to the infinite bus ($|V| = 1.0~pu$), with the generator terminal voltage ($|V_t| = 1.0~pu$). Calculate the generator emf behind transient reactance. Find the maximum power that can be transferred under the following conditions: (i) System healthy, (ii) One line shorted (3 phase) in the middle and (iii) One line open. Plot all the three power angle curves.
questions.method: $V_t$ angle from $P = V_tV\sin\theta/X$; current $I = (V_t - V)/jX$; $E' = V_t + jX'_dI$; $P_{max} = E'V/X_{transfer}$ for each network (fault: star-delta or Thevenin reduction).
draws: Diagram: network with the mid-line fault and its reduction
Graph: power-angle curves for the three cases

questions.label: 20-21 6(c)
questions.text: The generator of Fig. 2 is delivering 1.0 pu power to the infinite bus (|V|=1.0 pu), with the generator terminal voltage (|Vt|=1.0 pu). Calculate the generator emf behind transient reactance. Find the maximum power that can be transferred under the following conditions: (a) System healthy (b) One line shorted (3 phase) in the middle.
questions.method: $V_t$ angle from $P = V_tV\sin\theta/X$; current $I = (V_t - V)/jX$; $E' = V_t + jX'_dI$; $P_{max} = E'V/X_{transfer}$ for each network (fault: star-delta or Thevenin reduction).
questions.answer: $E' = 1.0747\angle33.94°$ pu; $P_{max}$ = 1.791 pu healthy, 0.693 pu with a mid-line fault
draws: Diagram: network with the mid-line fault and its reduction
Graph: power-angle curves

questions.label: 21-22 2(a)
questions.text: What is monopolar link?
questions.points: Monopolar HVDC link: one conductor (usually negative) between the converter stations, earth or sea as the return; cheap, used for submarine cables; bipolar and homopolar are the other kinds.
draws: Diagram: monopolar, bipolar and homopolar HVDC links
compare: Monopolar vs bipolar vs homopolar HVDC link: one conductor, earth return vs two conductors of opposite polarity vs two conductors of the same polarity, earth return

questions.label: 21-22 6(b)
questions.text: Define HVDC. Discuss the Economics of Power transmission.
questions.points: HVDC: power as high-voltage dc between a rectifier and an inverter station. Economics: Kelvin's law for conductor size (annual loss cost = annual capital charge on the area-dependent part), an economic voltage, and HVDC cheaper than HVAC beyond the break-even distance (lines and cables) despite costly terminals.
draws: Graph: Kelvin's law, capital charge and loss cost against area
Graph: total cost against distance for HVAC and HVDC
compare: HVDC vs HVAC transmission: costly terminals, cheap lines, no stability limit vs cheap terminals, reactive power, stability limit

questions.label: 21-22 2(b)
questions.text: Write down the general construction of a 3-conductor cable with required figure.
questions.points: From the centre: three stranded cores, each paper (or PVC/XLPE) insulated; jute fillers; a common paper belt; lead sheath; jute bedding; steel-wire or tape armour; jute serving.
draws: Diagram: cross-section of a three-core belted cable

questions.label: 21-22 2(d)
questions.text: Define grading of cables. Why is unequal stress distribution in a cable undesirable? Consider three dielectric layers for capacitance grading and derive the expression of potential difference between core and earthed sheath.
questions.outline: Gauss: $D_x = Q/2\pi x$ in every layer; $g_k = Q/(2\pi\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_kx)$; maximum at each inner surface; integrate each layer; add the three; equal maxima need $\varepsilon_1d = \varepsilon_2d_1 = \varepsilon_3d_2$.
draws: Diagram: cable with three dielectric layers and the stress profile
compare: Capacitance vs intersheath grading: layers of different permittivity vs metal intersheaths held at set voltages

questions.label: 21-22 4(d)
questions.text: A 66 kV single-core lead sheathed cable is graded by using two dielectrics of relative permittivity 5 and 3 respectively; thickness of each being 1 cm. The core diameter is 2 cm. Determine the maximum stress in the two dielectrics.
questions.method: The same $Q$ passes both layers, so $g_{2max}/g_{1max} = \varepsilon_1d/(\varepsilon_2d_1)$; $V = (g_{1max}d/2)\ln(d_1/d) + (g_{2max}d_1/2)\ln(D/d_1)$; solve for $g_{1max}$.
draws: Graph: stress across the graded and ungraded cable

questions.label: 21-22 3(b)
questions.text: What kind of line supports are used for distribution purposes at low voltages (upto 11 kV)?
questions.points: Wooden poles (cheap, spans of 40 to 50 m, rural), steel poles (rail or tubular, 50 to 80 m, towns), RCC poles (strong, long life, 80 to 200 m); A- or H-type double poles for heavy loads.

questions.label: 21-22 4(b)
questions.text: The insulation resistance of a single-core cable is 495 MΩ per km. If the core diameter is 2.5 cm and the resistivity of insulation is $4.5\times10^{14}~\Omega-cm$, find the insulation thickness.
questions.method: $R = (\rho/2\pi l)\ln(r_2/r_1)$; solve $\ln(r_2/r_1) = 2\pi lR/\rho$; thickness $r_2 - r_1$.
draws: Diagram: radial leakage current in the insulation

questions.label: 21-22 5(a)
questions.text: How Earth affect on transmission line capacitance?
questions.points: The earth is a zero-potential conductor; by the method of images it acts as equal and opposite charges at the same depth below ground; this raises the line capacitance slightly ($C = \pi\varepsilon_0/\ln[(d/r)\cdot2h/\sqrt{4h^2 + d^2}]$ for a single-phase line); small for high lines.
draws: Diagram: two-wire line above the earth with image charges

questions.label: 21-22 6(a)
questions.text: Find the most economical size of a single-core cable working on a 132 kV, 3- phase system, if a dielectric stress of 60 kV/cm can be allowed.
questions.method: Peak phase voltage $V = 132\sqrt2/\sqrt3$; most economical core $d = 2V/g_{max}$ (from $D/d = e$); sheath $D = ed$.
draws: Graph: sheath diameter against core diameter
